title: HNSW III: build one yourself
summary: Ninety lines of working HNSW, with layer sizes matching N/M^l exactly. Then a controlled comparison against the flat graph from Day 18 where the hierarchy contributed nothing at 2,800 vectors, which is a lesson about measuring at your own scale rather than trusting a paper's defaults.
html:
Two days of parts. Today they become an index: HNSW with layers, in about ninety lines, built and measured. Then a result I did not plan for, which is the most useful thing in the lesson.

Layer assignment

Each node gets a maximum layer from an exponentially decaying distribution. One line:

mL = 1.0 / math.log(M)

def random_layer(self):
    return int(-math.log(self.rng.random()) * mL)

That produces layer 0 for most nodes, layer 1 for about 1 in M, layer 2 for about 1 in M squared. The skip list coin flip from Day 17, with M faces instead of two. Built over 2,800 vectors at M=16:

actual layer sizes:  [2800, 180, 12, 2]
expected N / M^l:    [2800, 175,  11, 0.7]

No tuning, no correction. The distribution does what the arithmetic says it will.

Insertion

Three stages, and the asymmetry between them is the whole design:

# 1. descend from the top with a width-1 greedy walk, no connecting
ep = [self.entry]
for lv in range(self.max_layer, l, -1):
    found, _ = self._search_layer(vec, ep, 1, lv)
    ep = [found[0][1]]

# 2. at every layer this node belongs to, search properly and connect
for lv in range(min(l, self.max_layer), -1, -1):
    found, _ = self._search_layer(vec, ep, self.efc, lv)
    Ml = self.M0 if lv == 0 else self.M
    nbrs = self._select(vec, found, Ml)
    self.layers[lv][i] = list(nbrs)

    # 3. links are bidirectional, so prune the other side with the same rule
    for n in nbrs:
        self.layers[lv][n].append(i)
        if len(self.layers[lv][n]) > Ml:
            cs = sorted(((self._sim(x, self.X[n]), x)
                         for x in self.layers[lv][n]), reverse=True)
            self.layers[lv][n] = self._select(self.X[n], cs, Ml)
    ep = [n for _, n in found]

Note M0 = M * 2. Layer 0 holds every vector and does the actual work, so it gets double the connectivity. The upper layers only need to route.

Note also that the back-link pruning runs the same diversity rule, not a simple "drop the furthest". If you keep the nearest neighbours when a node overflows, you slowly collapse its edges into one direction and the graph stops being navigable. That detail is easy to skip and it quietly costs recall.

Search

def search(self, q, k=10, ef=64):
    ep = [self.entry]
    for lv in range(self.max_layer, 0, -1):          # coarse, width 1
        found, _ = self._search_layer(q, ep, 1, lv)
        ep = [found[0][1]]
    found, _ = self._search_layer(q, ep, max(ef, k), 0)   # the real search
    return [n for _, n in found[:k]]

Width 1 on the way down, width ef at the bottom. The upper layers are a lookup, not a search.

Two details that are easy to get wrong. During insertion the entry points carried into the next layer down are ep = [n for _, n in found], the whole candidate set, not just the best one. Passing a single node down narrows the search prematurely and costs recall for no saving. And the graph has exactly one global entry point, replaced whenever a node draws a higher layer than any seen so far. That is a single point of failure in the structural sense: if it ends up somewhere unrepresentative, every query starts its descent from a bad place, which is one reason production implementations take care over deleting it.

It works:

 efSearch  recall@10  visited  %corpus
       16      0.949      322    11.5%
       32      0.989      499    17.8%
       64      0.998      789    28.2%
      128      1.000     1216    43.4%

What ninety lines leaves out

This index is correct and it is not production. The gaps are worth naming, because each one is a day of someone's work in a real implementation:

  • Deletes. There are none. Yesterday's tombstone discussion has no implementation here at all.
  • Concurrency. Insertion mutates neighbour lists of existing nodes, so concurrent builds need per-node locking. Real implementations parallelise insertion and it is the fiddliest part of the code.
  • Memory layout. I store adjacency as Python lists in a dict. A real one packs edges into a flat array indexed by node so traversal is a contiguous read rather than a pointer chase, which matters enormously given Day 15's bandwidth argument.
  • Distance computation. Mine is a numpy dot per node. Production code does SIMD over batched candidates and prefetches the next neighbour list while scoring the current one.

The cost of all that shows in the build time. 2,800 vectors took 7.7 seconds here. Build is roughly O(N log N), so:

  100,000 vectors:  ~52x the work  ->  about  7 minutes in this Python
1,000,000 vectors: ~622x the work  ->  about 80 minutes in this Python

A C++ implementation with threaded insertion and SIMD distances runs that million-vector build in a couple of minutes. The factor of fifty is not algorithmic, it is all the things in the list above. Write this once to understand it, then use a real library.

The result I was not expecting

Day 18 built a flat graph, no layers. Same data, same M, same efConstruction, same queries. So I ran them against each other:

efSearch | HNSW rec  visited | flat rec  visited | difference
      16 |    0.949      322 |    0.957      305 |     -0.008
      32 |    0.989      499 |    0.990      472 |     -0.001
      64 |    0.998      789 |    0.999      750 |     -0.001
     128 |    1.000     1216 |    1.000     1165 |     -0.000

build:  hierarchical 7.7s    flat 5.3s

The hierarchy contributed nothing. The flat graph matched it on recall, visited slightly fewer nodes, and built 31 percent faster. I wrote the layers, they behaved exactly as specified, and they did not pay for themselves.

Why, and what not to conclude

The honest explanation is scale. The hierarchy's job is cutting the cost of getting near the right region, and that cost grows with corpus size while the fix grows as log N. At 2,800 vectors the descent is three layers and a flat graph with a decent entry point is already close enough. At a hundred million the entry problem is real and the descent is seven or eight layers.

So the correct reading is "the hierarchy did not pay for itself at 2,800 vectors", not "the hierarchy is useless". My corpus is three orders of magnitude below where this structure is aimed.

That said, this is a live question rather than my small-sample artefact. Published analysis has argued that the hierarchy contributes less than the original paper implies, particularly in high dimensions, and that flat navigable graphs with good entry point selection are competitive at surprisingly large scales. I have not reproduced those experiments and you should not take my 2,800 vectors as evidence either way about them. What I can say is that I measured it, got nothing, and the explanation that it is a log N effect at small N is consistent with the data rather than proven by it.

The transferable habit: when a paper's structure costs you something, measure whether it pays at your scale. Defaults are tuned for the problem the authors had.

What definitely earned its place in these ninety lines: beam search, which took recall from 0.163 to 0.95, and the diversity heuristic, without which the graph is not navigable at all. Those are the load bearing parts. The layers are an optimisation whose value depends on N.

You have now built the index that dominates in-memory vector search, and you know which of its pieces matter and why. Tomorrow is the other major family, the one that gives up graphs entirely and goes back to partitioning space: IVF.
exercise:
1. Break the diversity heuristic. In your own implementation, or by reading mine, replace _select with "keep the M nearest" and rebuild. Recall should fall noticeably at the same efSearch. That one function is the difference between a navigable graph and a collection of cliques, and feeling the drop is worth more than the explanation.

2. Check the layer distribution. Build at M=8, M=16 and M=32 and print the layer sizes each time. Confirm they track N divided by M to the power of the layer. If yours do not, your mL is wrong, and that is a bug that still produces a working index with a worse search path.

3. Run my comparison at your scale. If you have more vectors than I used, build flat and hierarchical with identical parameters and compare. You are looking for the corpus size where the hierarchy starts winning. That number is genuinely useful and I do not know what it is for your data.
